newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tajik foes sign peace accords.
newsitem.headline: Tajik foes sign peace accords.

text.p: The warring sides in Tajikistan's bitter four-year civil war signed two key accords on Monday aimed at securing peace in the former Soviet republic, Interfax news agency said.

The accords, signed by President Imomali Rakhmonov, Islamic opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri and a United Nations' envoy, map out the powers and functions of a new national reconciliation commission, it said.
Russian Prime Minister Vitkor Chernomyrdin, who was present at the signing ceremony in Moscow, said he was confident that both sides would strive to cement peace in Tajikistan.
"(These documents) reflect the aspirations of the whole Tajik people who are tired of war and feuds," Interfax quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.
Tens of thousands have been killed and many more displaced in fighting between the government and Islamic rebels, further complicated by seething regional and clan rivalries.

Under their agreement, the two sides undertake to complete negotiations for a permanent peace settlement by next July 1. They are expected to declare a general amnesty and to exchange prisoners of war, Interfax said.

The agency quoted Tajik government spokesman Zafar Saidov as saying the commission would bring opposition figures into all levels of government, prepare for a possible referendum on the constitution and possible parliamentary elections during a "transition period".
But it was unclear when elections or a referendum might be held in the war-torn country.
The opposition has in the past made known its desire to see such a commission form the basis of a power-sharing arrangement in the fragile Central Asian republic.
But diplomats have said the government could use the agreement to win time to strengthen its tenuous grip on power.
The rebels control the mountainous, eastern half of Tajikistan, although this is home to only around 10 percent of the population.
Instability in Tajikistan, which borders Afghanistan and China, formed the backdrop to the peace talks that began in Moscow last week.

Seven United Nations military observers were taken hostage by a Tajik guerrilla group on Friday but released on Saturday. There has been intermittent fighting in the centre of the republic despite a ceasefire agreed earlier this month.
Previous ceasefires have been routinely flouted. A U.N.-sponsored truce reconfirmed last July collapsed almost as soon as it was signed.
